chapter.title: Handling Events
chapter.description: Attaching handlers, the synthetic event object, and passing arguments.

blocks.text: React event props are camelCased and take a function, not a string. React attaches a single listener at the root of your app and dispatches events to your handlers itself.
`onClick={handleClick}` passes the function. `onClick={handleClick()}` calls it during render and passes the result, which almost never does what you want.
When a handler needs an argument, wrap it in an arrow function so the call happens at click time rather than at render time.

Handlers receive a **synthetic event**: a cross-browser wrapper with the same API as the native event. `event.target` is the element that fired it, and the native event is available as `event.nativeEvent`.
Call `event.preventDefault()` to stop a form submitting or a link navigating. Returning `false` from a React handler does nothing.
Put the handler on the `<form>`'s `onSubmit`, not the button's `onClick`. That way the Enter key works too, which matters for keyboard and screen reader users.
React events bubble up the component tree just like DOM events. `event.stopPropagation()` prevents a parent handler from also firing.

next.title: Conditional Rendering
next.description: Ternaries, logical AND, early returns and when to use each.

blocks.text: There is no special syntax for conditionals in JSX. You use ordinary JavaScript, and pick whichever form reads best.
Logical AND: show it or show nothing

Always make the left side a real boolean. `{unreadCount &&

...

}` renders a bare `0` on screen when the count is zero, because 0 is falsy but still renderable.
Early return: skip the whole component
When a component should render nothing, or something entirely different, return early. It keeps the main path free of nesting.

blocks.caption: Handle the exceptional cases first, then render the normal one.

blocks.text: For more than two or three branches, an object lookup is usually clearer than nested ternaries.
